### GET /v1/report

The whole-capture analysis: findings across every dialog and stream, orphaned
media, STUN and ICMP evidence, and what the retention caps shed.

`GET /v1/dialogs/{call_id}/report` answers for one call. This answers for the
capture.

- It is the only REST route that can.
- Orphaned media and shed
  retention belong to no single dialog.
- So every other route is blind to them.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/report | jq .
```

**Read `complete` before the findings.** It is `false` when the capture:

- lost packets,
- hit a retention cap, or
- held frames no decoder could read.

A findings list built from such a capture is a **floor, not a
total**. A reader who takes the list at face value concludes the capture is
clean when it is merely partial.

`dialogs_examined` and `streams_examined` are the denominators behind the
findings. `frames_read` is the count `/metrics` reports as
`sipnab_capture_packets_total`.

The body is the capture analysis itself, the object `--json-analyze` prints.
It opens with `schema_version`.

- The published contract is
  [`tests/schemas/capture_analysis.schema.json`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/tests/schemas/capture_analysis.schema.json),
  spliced into the OpenAPI document as `CaptureReport`.
- `filter` never appears
  here. This route analyzes every dialog in the store.

**Query parameter:**

| Name | Legal values | If omitted |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | `json`, or `yang-json` for the same analysis [RFC 7951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7951.html)-encoded against the YANG module `sipnab-diagnosis`. Anything else is a `400`. | `json` |

`?format=yang-json` answers `Content-Type: application/yang-data+json`. That is the
media type [RFC 8040](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8040.html) registers for YANG data. The body validates against the
module `sipnab --print-yang-module` prints:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  'http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/report?format=yang-json' > analysis.json
```

```bash
yanglint -t data sipnab-diagnosis@2026-10-09.yang analysis.json
```

It is the same analysis in a different encoding. The YANG section of
[Output formats](@/docs/output-formats.md) lists every difference.

This is not a
RESTCONF server. The route, the guard and the bearer token are the ones every
other route uses.

The MCP `get_capture_report` tool answers the same question, with the same
`format` spellings.

- So do `sipnab --analyze`, `--json-analyze` and
  `--yang-analyze` on the command line.
- `--report` does not. It is the tabular
  per-dialog summary and ranks nothing.

---

### GET /v1/runtime

What sipnab is doing, and what it is costing the host it runs on.

sipnab exports 45 Prometheus metrics. The listener that serves them is off
by default.

- This endpoint answers the same questions without that listener.
- It also reports:
  - sipnab's own resource use,
  - its share of the machine.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/runtime | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "process": {
    "rss_bytes": 34471936,
    "virtual_bytes": 1276837888,
    "threads": 2,
    "open_fds": 12,
    "cpu_seconds": 0.01
  },
  "host": {
    "memory_total_bytes": 131881889792,
    "memory_available_bytes": 121499242496,
    "cpus": 14,
    "basis": "host"
  },
  "impact": {
    "memory_pct": 0.026,
    "significant": false,
    "note": "sipnab holds 0.0% of the host memory total; the threshold for load-bearing is 10.0%"
  },
  "interfaces": [],
  "dialogs": { "used": 2, "capacity": 100000, "pct": 0.002 },
  "streams": { "used": 2, "capacity": 10000, "pct": 0.02 },
  "capture_sources": { "used": 1, "capacity": 65536, "pct": 0.0015 },
  "capture_sources_refused_total": 0,
  "capture_packets_total": 852,
  "capture_queue_depth_packets": 0,
  "capture_backpressure_blocks_total": 0,
  "uptime_seconds": 41,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

On a `--hep-send` run the envelope also carries `hep_export`. It shows what the exporter
delivered, replayed, dropped and failed:

```json
"hep_export": {
  "transport": "tcp",
  "packets_sent": 18204,
  "failures": { "connect": 3, "tls_handshake": 0, "write": 0 },
  "reconnects": 1,
  "queued": 18210,
  "replayed": 212,
  "dropped": { "queue_full": 0, "stopped": 0, "unsent_at_exit": 0 },
  "queue_depth": 6,
  "delivery": "written to the connection: a write that fails is counted, the packet stays queued, and the sender dials again with backoff"
}
```

Every failure kind and every drop reason appears, zeros included.

- A failure is one failed delivery attempt. The packet stays queued and the
  sender tries it again, so losses are the `dropped` counts.
- `connect` is a collector that
  refused, or that the sender could not reach within `--hep-send-timeout`.
- `tls_handshake` is
  a collector whose certificate the sender does not accept.
- `write` is a packet
  an established connection refused.
- `queued` always equals `packets_sent` plus every `dropped` count plus
  `queue_depth`.

See [When the `--hep-send` collector goes
away](@/docs/cli.md#when-the-hep-send-collector-goes-away).

**Over UDP, `packets_sent` means handed to
the kernel.** A collector that is down produces no failure at all. `delivery` says
this in words. The key is absent on a run that exports nothing.

**An absent field means "not readable here", never zero.**

- Every value under
  `process` and `host` is optional because the sources are platform-specific.
- A field reported as `0` on a platform where it was never read is worse than one
  that says it does not know.

**`host.basis` names the denominator.**

- Inside a container, the real limits are
  the control group's limits rather than the machine's.
- So the basis reads
  `cgroup` and the totals
  come from `memory.max`.
- A percentage computed against the wrong total is worse
  than no percentage, because a reader believes it.

**`impact.significant` says whether sipnab's memory use is large enough to
affect the host.** It is `true` when sipnab holds at least the threshold share
of host memory. `note` states the share and the threshold.

**`interfaces` reads the interface, not the capture handle.**

- sipnab's own
  counters (`ps_recv`, `ps_drop`, `ps_ifdrop`) describe what reached sipnab.
- These describe what reached the NIC.
- The pair is what separates the two
  remedies:
  - `ps_ifdrop` climbing alongside `rx_missed_errors` is hardware that
    cannot keep up. The fix is ring size, coalescing or RSS.
  - `ps_drop` climbing
    alone is sipnab's read loop falling behind. The fix is `--buffer` or a
    tighter filter.
- The handle counter on its own cannot tell you which.

**The capture-queue fields are absent without a capture.**

- A run replaying a
  file through the API owns no capture meter.
- So `capture_queue_depth_packets`
  and `capture_backpressure_blocks_total` do not appear at all. They do not
  appear as `0`.
- Zero there would read as "the queue is clear". That is the one thing a
  saturated pipeline must never say.

**Occupancy, not just counts.** `dialogs.used` alone is a number. Beside
`capacity` it is a decision. An operator who cannot see occupancy learns about
eviction by noticing that calls have gone missing.

**Rates are opt-in, because measuring one costs a wait.** Every counter above
is cumulative. "1,284,301 messages" answers a different question from "312
messages/second, of which 190 are OPTIONS". Add `?sample_seconds=N` to read the
counters twice across an `N`-second window:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/runtime?sample_seconds=5" | jq .rates
```

```json
{
  "window_seconds": 5,
  "packets_per_second": 412.6,
  "calls_per_second": 3.4,
  "calls_per_second_by_method": [
    ["OPTIONS", 2.8],
    ["INVITE", 0.6]
  ]
}
```

`calls_per_second_by_method` separates INVITE from OPTIONS, so keepalive
traffic does not hide the call rate.

`window_seconds` is the window sipnab **applied**, not the one you asked for.

- The request waits out the window before answering.
- So sipnab narrows a window
  longer than this route can answer inside its request timeout.
- `window_seconds` tells you that happened.

sipnab rejects `sample_seconds=0`
rather than answering it.

- An empty window returns zero deltas.
- Zero deltas
  is exactly what a healthy quiet capture looks like.

The MCP tool `runtime_stats` returns the same envelope, with the same refusal
and the same clamp.

### GET /v1/hep/senders

This route shows:

- who is feeding this run's HEP listener,
- who went silent,
- who it is turning away.

It exists only in a build with the `hep` feature. It needs a full-scope token.
Sender addresses describe your estate, so a `metrics` token gets `401`.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/hep/senders | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "listening": true,
  "trust": "shared_secret_plain",
  "silence_threshold_seconds": 30,
  "packets_received": 1843,
  "packets_admitted": 1829,
  "packets_refused": 14,
  "refused_by_reason": {
    "allowlist": 0, "auth_missing": 0, "auth_mismatch": 14, "hmac_bad_format": 0,
    "hmac_bad_mac": 0, "hmac_replay": 0, "hmac_timestamp_out_of_window": 0,
    "hmac_unsupported_version": 0, "malformed": 0, "peer_tracking_full": 0,
    "rate_limit_global": 0, "rate_limit_per_peer": 0
  },
  "senders_tracked": 2,
  "senders_limit": 4096,
  "senders_silent": 1,
  "untracked_packets": 0,
  "senders": [
    {
      "source": "hep:7@192.0.2.7", "capture_id": 7, "peer": "192.0.2.7",
      "identity": "claimed_by_sender", "trust": "shared_secret_plain",
      "packets": 1604, "first_seen": "2026-09-21T12:00:00.412Z",
      "last_seen": "2026-09-21T12:14:59.880Z", "idle_seconds": 0, "silent": false
    },
    {
      "source": "hep:9@192.0.2.9", "capture_id": 9, "peer": "192.0.2.9",
      "identity": "claimed_by_sender", "trust": "shared_secret_plain",
      "packets": 225, "first_seen": "2026-09-21T12:00:01.020Z",
      "last_seen": "2026-09-21T12:09:12.334Z", "idle_seconds": 348, "silent": true
    }
  ],
  "refused_sources_tracked": 1,
  "refused_sources_limit": 256,
  "refused_sources_evicted": 0,
  "refused_sources": [
    {
      "peer": "203.0.113.66", "packets": 14, "by_reason": { "auth_mismatch": 14 },
      "first_seen": "2026-09-21T12:03:40.101Z", "last_seen": "2026-09-21T12:14:58.007Z"
    }
  ]
}
```

**A sender is the capture id it claims and the address it sent from.**

- Two proxies that both leave `--hep-id` at its default of 1 are still two rows.
- One host running two sipnab agents with different ids is two rows too.
- `source` is the same `hep:<capture-id>@<peer>` string every frame pointer from that
  sender carries. So a row and a pointer name one sender the same way.

**`identity` is always `claimed_by_sender`.**

- One shared secret serves the
  whole listener.
- sipnab asks no sender for a client certificate.
- So any sender holding the secret can claim any capture id.
- The roster reports what senders say about
  themselves, and says so.

**`silent`, never "down".** A sender is silent once it has sent nothing sipnab
admitted for `silence_threshold_seconds` (`--hep-silence-warn`).

- A PBX with no
  calls at night may legitimately send nothing.
- So the word describes what
  sipnab saw, not what happened to the sender.
- Only admitted packets count. A
  sender whose packets now fail authentication goes silent. It shows up under
  `refused_sources` instead.

**The refused-source table keys on address alone.** A refused packet proved
nothing, including the capture id it claimed.

- The table holds the 256 addresses
  refused most recently and evicts the oldest.
- So a spoofed flood rotates it
  rather than freezing it.
- `refused_by_reason` counts every refusal, and nothing
  evicts it.

**Both lists have bounds, and the totals beside them do not.**

- The sender
  table holds `senders_limit` senders (`[limits] max_tracked_peers`).
- A sender arriving after it fills still reaches the capture and counts in
  `untracked_packets`. But it gets no row.
- The table refuses new entries rather than
  recycling old ones, because it also numbers each sender's frames.
- `?limit=N` caps the rows each list returns without changing any total.

**No listener, no roster.** A run without `-L` answers `listening: false`, zero
counts and a `note`. It never answers with an empty roster that would read as "nobody is
sending".

The MCP tool `hep_senders` returns the same fields and values for the same
roster, with its keys in alphabetical order and `source_exhausted` and
`source_stopped_early` added.
`--hep-senders` prints it at the end of a headless run. Prometheus carries only
the aggregate counts, with no per-sender label. See
[Metrics](@/docs/metrics.md).

### GET /v1/capabilities

What this build can do and what the operator turned on. This is the machine contract a
program reads before it asks. With it, a refusal it could have predicted does not read
as a dead end.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/capabilities | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "version": "0.5.175",
  "features": ["api", "audio", "bpf", "hep", "mcp", "metrics", "native", "tls", "tui", "vcon"],
  "can_decrypt": true,
  "can_hep": true,
  "can_plugins": false,
  "runtime": {
    "api_allow_relay_query": false,
    "api_allow_vcon_fetch": false
  },
  "libpcap": {
    "banner": "libpcap version 1.10.5 (with TPACKET_V3)",
    "version": "1.10.5",
    "named_backends": []
  }
}
```

**`features` is the one canonical list.**

- It is the same set `--version` prints and
  the MCP `server_capabilities` tool returns.
- It names only features compiled into the running binary.
- A capability absent here is one this build cannot do.
  That is a different fact from one this run did not turn on.

**`runtime` names what the operator turned on.**

- Some routes answer
  `not_permitted` because `--api-allow-relay-query` was not passed. That is not a
  missing feature.
- A program that blurs the two retries something that can
  never work.
- `api_allow_relay_query` is off unless this run may transmit a relay
  query.
- `api_allow_vcon_fetch` is off unless
  [`GET /v1/vcon/fetch/:uuid`](#get-v1-vcon-fetch-uuid) can reach a store: the run
  has `--api-allow-vcon-fetch` and the config file sets `[vcon_fetch] url`.

**`libpcap` names the library this process captures through**, as the
library reports itself at runtime.

- A gnu build or a package reports the
  host's libpcap. The sample above is Debian 13's.
- A static musl build
  reports the 1.10.6 it carries.

`named_backends` lists the alternate capture
backends (`netmap`, `dpdk`, `dag`, `snf`) that the banner names. It is
`[]` when the banner names none. That is not proof the library has none:

- libpcap names netmap in
  its banner only from 1.10.6,
- and DPDK only in a DPDK-only build.

See [which
capture backends an artifact can
reach](@/docs/install.md#which-capture-backends-an-artifact-can-reach).

The MCP tool `server_capabilities` returns the same feature set and the same
`libpcap` block. The second line of `sipnab --version` prints the same
library banner.

### GET /v1/stats

Aggregate statistics across all dialogs and streams, including PDD percentiles.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/stats | jq .
```

**Python:**

<!-- snippet: clients/python/stats.py#stats -->
```python
req = Request(
    f"{BASE}/v1/stats",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
)
with urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:
    stats = json.load(resp)
d = stats["dialogs"]
print(f"Dialogs: {d['total']} total, {d['active']} active, {d['failed']} failed")
t = stats["timing"]
print(f"PDD: p50={t['pdd_p50_ms']}ms, p95={t['pdd_p95_ms']}ms")
```

**Go:**

<!-- snippet: clients/go/stats/main.go#stats -->
```go
req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/stats", nil)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
	return fmt.Errorf("GET /v1/stats: %s", resp.Status)
}

var stats struct {
	Dialogs struct {
		Total  int `json:"total"`
		Active int `json:"active"`
		Failed int `json:"failed"`
	} `json:"dialogs"`
}
if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&stats); err != nil {
	return err
}
d := stats.Dialogs
fmt.Printf("Dialogs: %d total, %d active, %d failed\n", d.Total, d.Active, d.Failed)
```

**JavaScript (Node.js):**

<!-- snippet: clients/javascript/stats.mjs#stats -->
```javascript
const resp = await fetch(`${base}/v1/stats`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
});
if (!resp.ok) throw new Error(`GET /v1/stats: ${resp.status} ${resp.statusText}`);
const stats = await resp.json();
const { dialogs, timing } = stats;
console.log(`Dialogs: ${dialogs.total} total, ${dialogs.active} active`);
console.log(`PDD p50: ${timing.pdd_p50_ms}ms, p95: ${timing.pdd_p95_ms}ms`);
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 2,
  "dialogs": {
    "total": 1247,
    "active": 23,
    "in_call": 9,
    "completed": 1180,
    "failed": 32,
    "canceled": 12
  },
  "streams": {
    "total": 46,
    "orphaned": 3
  },
  "caveats": {
    "media_creating_commands": 0
  },
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture01",
    "instance": "1f4a17c8e2b91d40-1",
    "dialog_generation": 412,
    "stream_generation": 96
  },
  "source": "live",
  "capture_name": "eth0",
  "uptime_sec": 3600,
  "source_exhausted": false,
  "writing_to": null,
  "unsaved": true,
  "unanalysed_sip_messages": 0,
  "unanalysed_busiest_ports": [],
  "unanalysed_websocket_messages": 0,
  "unanalysed_websocket_ports": [],
  "timing": {
    "pdd_p50_ms": 120,
    "pdd_p95_ms": 850,
    "pdd_p99_ms": 2100
  },
  "capture_quality": {
    "kernel_dropped_packets": 0,
    "interface_dropped_packets": 0,
    "invalid_timestamps": 0,
    "undecodable_frames": 0,
    "snapped_frames": 0,
    "unanswered_nat_requests": 0,
    "lapsed_turn_allocations": 0,
    "lapsed_turn_allocation_streams": 0,
    "ice_role_conflicts": 0,
    "degraded": false
  }
}
```

`caveats` is the other half of that question, and it reads the opposite way.
`capture_quality` counts what the capture **lost**. `caveats` counts what
sipnab **declined**.

| Key | What it counts |
|-----|----------------|
| `media_creating_commands` | rtpengine `subscribe`, `publish` and `start recording` commands seen and deliberately not attributed |
| `tls` | TLS decryption state — **absent** unless a decryptor ran |

Those commands create media for a call without being one of its two legs.
sipnab does not attribute that media to the call, so a two-party call keeps
two streams and its one-way-audio and asymmetry checks stay valid. A non-zero
`media_creating_commands` means such media existed and is not in the call's
streams.

**`media_creating_commands` is always present, and `0` is a real answer.**

#### `caveats.tls` — is decryption working?

Absent when nobody supplied keys. That is not a decryption failure.
Flattening it into a report of zeroes would make it look like one.

When a decryptor ran:

```json
"tls": {
  "keylog_entries": 4,
  "sessions_with_keys": 1,
  "app_data_records": 900,
  "decrypted_records": 895,
  "undecrypted_records": 5,
  "late_recovered": 0,
  "late_evicted": 0,
  "read_nothing": false
}
```

**Read `read_nothing`, not the arithmetic.**

- A TLS handshake carries records
  sipnab never loads keys for.
- So `app_data_records > decrypted_records` is not by
  itself a failure.
- Deriving a verdict from the two counts sends an operator
  after keys that already work.
- `read_nothing` is `true` only for the unambiguous
  case: application data arrived and none of it opened.

That case is the reason this block exists.

- A capture holding ciphertext nobody
  can open produces a dialog listing identical to one from a quiet network.
- Without this number, there is nothing on the page to tell them apart.

`late_recovered` and `late_evicted` stay separate. "We never had the
keys" and "we had them and had already discarded the ciphertext" are different
problems.

- A larger hold fixes the second.
- Supplying keys fixes the first.

The counts are cumulative for the process. sipnab publishes them as
decryption happens. So a client can read them mid-run. It does not need to wait for
the end-of-run summary the command line prints.

The MCP `capture_status` tool carries the same block under the same name, so
this endpoint and an agent never disagree about it.

### Which capture these counts came from

`capture_identity` pairs the capture's instance with both store generations.
Compare it across calls:

- **higher generation, same instance** — the capture grew
- **different instance** — something swapped the file. Every count you
  were holding describes a different capture.

It is the **same identity** the MCP `capture_status` tool stamps its answers
with, read from the same object.

- An agent and an HTTP client polling one
  process can therefore tell they are describing one capture.
- Both see a swap the moment it happens.

sipnab reads the instance and both generations at the same moment.

`null` when nobody told this server what capture it holds.

**These answers carry `capture_identity`:** `GET /v1/dialogs`,
`/v1/dialogs/{call_id}`, `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/report`,
`/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/correlated`, `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/tree`,
`/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/lint`, `/v1/dialogs/compare`, `/v1/dialogs/tail`,
`/v1/dialogs/rates`, `/v1/streams`, `/v1/streams/{id}`, `/v1/report`,
`/v1/stats`, `/v1/aggregate`, `/v1/timeline`, `/v1/talkers`, `/v1/endpoints`,
`/v1/runtime` and `/v1/security/findings`.
Each one carries the identity the MCP tool answering the same question
carries, read under the same locks as the answer. These answers do not carry it:

| Answer | Why |
|---|---|
| `/v1/report?format=yang-json` | RFC 7951 allows no member at the top of the document that its YANG module does not declare. Request `format=json` for the identity. |
| `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` | The body is the vCon container itself. MCP `export_vcon` puts the identity on the envelope around its containers. |
| `/v1/hep/senders` | The MCP `hep_senders` tool does not carry it either: the answer is the HEP listener's sender roster, not the capture's contents. |
| `/v1/capabilities`, `/v1/captures/compare`, `/v1/vcon/spool`, `/v1/vcon/fetch/{uuid}`, `/v1/tfps/*`, `/v1/relay/*` | The answer is not about the loaded capture: it describes the build, two files on the file root, the spool, the vCon store, the TFPS peer, or the media relay. |
| `/v1/persistence`, `/v1/calls/live` | No MCP tool answers the same question. |
| `/health`, `/metrics`, the audio routes | They answer text or audio, not a JSON object. |

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `source` | `live`, `file`, or `unknown` |
| `capture_name` | interface name when live, file path when replaying |
| `uptime_sec` | seconds since capture began |
| `source_exhausted` | `true` once sipnab reaches the end of a file source |
| `writing_to` | path sipnab saves packets to, if any |
| `unsaved` | `true` only for a **live** capture with no output file — packets held in memory and nowhere else |

**`unknown` is a real answer, not a default.** sipnab reports `unknown`
rather than guess `live` or `file`.

Read `unsaved` before you stop a capture.

- A file replay is already
  on disk, so it is never unsaved.
- A live capture with an output file is safe to
  stop.

### Find SIP that `--portrange` excluded

sipnab reads SIP only on the ports `--portrange` names (default `5060-5061`).
When it reads a file, it counts the SIP it skipped on other ports and names
those ports. `capture_quality` does not include this count: sipnab lost no packet, and
it recognized the bytes as SIP.

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `unanalysed_sip_messages` | plain SIP with both ports outside `--portrange` |
| `unanalysed_busiest_ports` | the top five ports carrying it, busiest first |
| `unanalysed_websocket_messages` | SIP-over-WebSocket ([RFC 7118](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7118.html)) outside the WebSocket port set |
| `unanalysed_websocket_ports` | the top five ports carrying that |

To check a server, read the four keys from `/v1/stats`. This server replays
[`tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/raw/main/tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap) with `--portrange 5070-5080`, a range
that excludes the capture's SIP port:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/stats \
  | jq '{dialogs: .dialogs.total, unanalysed_sip_messages, unanalysed_busiest_ports}'
```

```json
{
  "dialogs": 0,
  "unanalysed_sip_messages": 23,
  "unanalysed_busiest_ports": [
    {
      "messages": 23,
      "port": 5060
    }
  ]
}
```

`dialogs` is `0` because every SIP message was on port 5060. To analyze them,
restart sipnab with a range that covers the listed ports, for example
`--portrange 5060-5061`, or `--portrange 1-65535` for every port.

For SIP over WebSocket, widening `--portrange` does not help. Set
`--ws-portrange` to the ports `unanalysed_websocket_ports` lists. This is
common behind a reverse proxy that terminates WSS, and with Kamailio, OpenSIPS
and Janus, whose WebSocket ports are outside sipnab's default
80/443/8080/8443.

Both counts are `0` on a live capture. There, the port range becomes the BPF
filter, and the kernel drops other ports before sipnab sees them.

MCP `capture_status` carries all four under the same names.

`capture_quality` says how much of the wire the rest of the response draws
from. Read it before the counts, not after. With `degraded` true:

- every number
  above it is a floor rather than a total,
- the `timing` percentiles may rest
  on substituted clock readings.

The three counters stay apart because their remedies disagree:

- **`kernel_dropped_packets`** — the capture ring was full when the packet
  arrived. Raise `-B`/`--buffer`, narrow the BPF filter, or cut `--snaplen`.
- **`interface_dropped_packets`** — the NIC or its driver discarded the packet
  before libpcap saw it. Look at the NIC, the driver or the mirror. **A bigger
  buffer cannot recover these.**
- **`invalid_timestamps`** — the pcap timestamp was unusable. So the packet
  carries the wall clock instead. Nothing went missing. But treat post-dial delay,
  jitter, MOS and duration for this run as unreliable.

`undecodable_frames` is a fourth channel. It is the only one that is about sipnab
rather than the host.

- Nothing dropped it and no byte is missing.
- The frames arrived intact and no decoder here could read them.
- So the analysis saw none of
  their contents.
- It is what separates *this capture holds no SIP* from *sipnab
  could not read this capture*. Both otherwise report `dialogs.total`
  as `0`.

Which link types, EtherTypes and IP protocols this covers appears in
`sipnab_capture_undecodable_frames_total{reason}` on `/metrics`. The
proportion is `sipnab_capture_undecoded_fraction`.

It is **not** part of `degraded`. ARP frames count as undecodable, and nearly
every Ethernet capture holds some.

`snapped_frames` is a fifth channel. It is neither loss nor a decode failure.

- The frames arrived, and most of them decoded.
- What is missing is payload.
- That is exactly what a signaling-only capture sets out to discard.

It matters because
the `--snaplen` warnings fire once per run. They cannot say how MUCH of a capture
came in truncated.

- A run that decoded every packet and snapped 94% of them is
  not a clean capture.
- No other key here says so.
- Raise `--snaplen` when you
  need RTP payload, audio export, or a faithful `-O` re-emit.

The last four keys are the only ones in this block about the **network** rather
than about the capture. Those frames arrived perfectly. What each key
describes went wrong on the wire:

| Key | What it counts, and what to do about it |
|---|---|
| `unanswered_nat_requests` | STUN and TURN transactions that went out and never came back — the signal behind a one-way-audio complaint. An endpoint that cannot learn its reflexive address (the public `address:port` a NAT gives it, which STUN exists to discover) advertises its private address in SDP, and the far end then sends media somewhere the internet cannot route, while the signaling looks healthy. Silence rather than a refusal points at something in the path discarding UDP it does not recognize, most often a firewall, IPS or secure web gateway. A refusal counts as answered: the server was reachable and said no, which is a different fault |
| `lapsed_turn_allocations` | TURN allocations still carrying traffic past the lifetime the server last granted them, with no Refresh seen in between. The one fault here with no other symptom anywhere — the relay tears the allocation down the moment its lifetime lapses, the relayed media stops with it mid-call, and no SIP message says why. A deliberate release (a Refresh with `LIFETIME` 0) never counts, because the client asked for the teardown |
| `lapsed_turn_allocation_streams` | Media streams crossing an allocation that had already lapsed. The scale beside the key above, and the reason that key is worth paging on: an allocation that lapsed with nothing on it cost nobody a call, and one carrying four streams cut off four conversations mid-sentence |
| `ice_role_conflicts` | Candidate pairs where both ICE agents claimed the same role, or where one answered `487 Role Conflict` ([RFC 8445 section 7.3.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445.html#section-7.3.1.1)). ICE resolves this itself, so a single conflict is not always fatal — which is why it belongs on a dashboard rather than only in an alert. Where no pair between the two ever won nomination, the conflict is a candidate cause of media that never started |

All four fall as well as rise.

- A late answer, a Refresh that arrives afterwards
  or a later nomination each removes one.
- So read them as current readings rather
  than as running totals.
- [Prometheus Metrics](@/docs/metrics.md) publishes
  the same four numbers as gauges for a scrape.

Neither `snapped_frames` nor any of those four counts toward `degraded`.
It stays a statement about packets this host lost.

`degraded` is `true` when any of the three is non-zero.

- `false` means nothing
  was *observed* to go wrong.
- It does not mean the capture provably saw every packet.
- Loss upstream of the capture point is invisible to
  all three counters. Examples:
  - an oversubscribed SPAN port,
  - a tap mirroring one direction,
  - a filter that excluded the traffic.

---

### GET /v1/aggregate

How many dialogs, grouped by one dimension. This is the "how many, by what" question,
answered over the store rather than the model.

**Query parameters:**

- `by` (required) — the dimension: one of `state`, `response_code`, `method`,
  `from.user`, `to.user`, `ua`, `src.ip`, `dst.ip`, `rtp.codec`. A key outside
  that set is a `400`.
- `filter` (optional) — a DSL expression or named alias narrowing which
  dialogs the count includes, what `/v1/dialogs?filter=` accepts. A value that
  is neither is a `400`.
- `top_n` (optional) — keep the largest N buckets. The rest fold into
  `other_count`.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/aggregate?by=response_code" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "group_by": "response_code",
  "buckets": [
    { "value": "200", "count": 412 },
    { "value": "486", "count": 19 },
    { "value": "(none)", "count": 7 }
  ],
  "other_count": 0,
  "distinct_values": 3,
  "total_matched": 438,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**One dimension at a time.** Narrow with `filter` rather than asking for a
second.

- The buckets are largest first.
- Value breaks ties, so the same store
  always gives the same answer.
- `other_count` carries everything past `top_n`.
  So the buckets plus it sum to `total_matched`.
- A `(none)` bucket counts the
  dialogs with no value for the dimension.
  - "How many carry no User-Agent" is a
    real question.
  - Dropping them would break the sum.

The MCP tool `aggregate_dialogs` answers from the same `GROUPABLE` dimensions and
the same bucketing rule (`dialog_group_value_raw`).

- It fences the sender-controlled
  values for a model.
- This route returns them raw for a program.

---

### GET /v1/timeline

How many calls opened over time, in fixed-width buckets. This is the volume series a
dashboard polls.

**Query parameters:**

- `bucket_seconds` (optional) — the interval width, default 60. Zero is a `400`.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/timeline?bucket_seconds=300" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "buckets": [
    { "start": "2026-09-15T12:00:00+00:00", "bucket_seconds": 300, "dialogs": 42 },
    { "start": "2026-09-15T12:05:00+00:00", "bucket_seconds": 300, "dialogs": 0 },
    { "start": "2026-09-15T12:10:00+00:00", "bucket_seconds": 300, "dialogs": 51 }
  ],
  "returned": 3,
  "bucket_seconds": 300,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**Buckets align to the epoch, not to the first call.** So two captures line up
on the same boundaries.

- The series keeps every empty interval rather than
  discarding it.
- An empty bucket is exactly what an outage looks like.
- Discarding one would hide the gap.

The MCP tool `timeline` buckets the same way.

---

### GET /v1/dialogs/compare

Two calls side by side, with the fields that differ named for you. This is the same
comparison the MCP `compare_dialogs` tool answers.

**Query parameters:**

- `a` (required) — Call-ID of the first call. A Call-ID with no dialog is a `404`.
- `b` (required) — Call-ID of the second call. A Call-ID with no dialog is a `404`.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/compare?a=call-a@example.com&b=call-b@example.com" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "a": {
    "call_id": "call-a@example.com",
    "state": "InCall",
    "final_status_code": 200,
    "msg_count": 7,
    "methods": ["ACK", "BYE", "INVITE"],
    "hints": []
  },
  "b": {
    "call_id": "call-b@example.com",
    "state": "Failed",
    "final_status_code": 486,
    "msg_count": 3,
    "methods": ["INVITE"],
    "hints": ["the callee was busy"]
  },
  "differences": ["state", "final_status_code", "msg_count", "methods"],
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**`differences` names the fields that moved.**

- It is a subset of `state`,
  `final_status_code`, `msg_count` and `methods`, in that order.
- It is empty when the
  two calls match on all four.
- A client that diffs the two itself sometimes
  reports a difference that is not there. So the route names them.
- `hints` rides
  along per side but stays out of the diff.

---

### GET /v1/dialogs/tail

The dialogs that changed since your last poll. This is cursor-based change tracking.

- It is the pattern a monitoring system reaches for.
- The `/v1/dialogs`
  offset pagination cannot express it.
- It is the same question the MCP `tail_dialogs` tool
  answers.

**Query parameters:**

- `since` (optional) — the previous response's `next_cursor`, passed back
  verbatim. The route returns only dialogs updated strictly after it. Omit it on the
  first poll. A cursor whose timestamp half is not [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html) is a `400`.
- `limit` (optional) — the most rows to return, clamped to the server's row cap.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/tail" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "dialogs": [
    { "call_id": "a@example.com", "state": "InCall", "updated_at": "2026-09-15T12:00:03Z" }
  ],
  "returned": 1,
  "next_cursor": "2026-09-15T12:00:03Z|a@example.com",
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**The rows are the same summaries `/v1/dialogs` returns,** oldest update first.

- Pass `next_cursor` back as `since` on the next poll. Only later changes come
  back.
- The cursor renders its timestamp as `Z` rather than `+00:00`.
  So it drops straight into the `since` query. A raw `+` there decodes to a space.
- A tie
  group sharing one update instant resumes on the `(timestamp, Call-ID)` pair.
  So a page boundary inside it neither repeats nor skips a row.
- `next_cursor` is null
  when nothing changed.

---

### GET /v1/dialogs/rates

Carrier metrics per group, grouped by one dimension:

- ASR, NER, ACD,
- post-dial-delay percentiles,
- MOS p10,
- a retransmit rate.

This is the scorecard a monitoring
system polls. `/v1/aggregate` bare counts cannot express it. These are the same figures
the MCP `group_dialogs` tool computes.

**Query parameters:**

- `by` (required) — the ONE dimension to group by: the fields `/v1/aggregate`
  counts by (`state`, `response_code`, `method`, `from.user`, `to.user`, `ua`,
  `src.ip`, `dst.ip`, `rtp.codec`) plus `to_domain`, `hour` and `next_hop`. A
  key outside that set is a `400`.
- `metrics` (optional) — a comma-separated subset of `count`, `asr`, `ner`,
  `acd`, `pdd_p50`, `pdd_p95`, `mos_p10`, `retransmit_rate`. Defaults to all. An
  unknown name is a `400`.
- `filter` (optional) — a DSL expression or named alias narrowing which
  dialogs the route groups, what `/v1/dialogs?filter=` accepts. A value that is
  neither is a `400`.
- `top_n` (optional) — keep the largest N groups by dialog count. The rest fold
  into `other_count`. Clamped to the server's row cap.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/rates?by=next_hop&metrics=asr,ner,acd" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "group_by": "next_hop",
  "metrics": ["acd", "asr", "ner"],
  "units": { "acd": "seconds", "asr": "percent", "ner": "percent" },
  "groups": [
    {
      "value": "203.0.113.9:5060",
      "count": 120,
      "metrics": { "asr": 71.67, "ner": 95.0, "acd": 182.4 },
      "not_grounded": {},
      "population": {
        "dialogs": 120, "seizures": 120, "answered": 86, "delivered": 114,
        "completed_calls": 86, "pdd_measured": 118, "mos_grounded_dialogs": 0,
        "retransmits": 4
      }
    }
  ],
  "other_count": 0,
  "distinct_values": 1,
  "total_matched": 120,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**Every figure carries the population behind it.**

- A metric its
  population cannot support comes back null, with the reason in `not_grounded`.
  It does not come back as a zero.
- An ASR of zero over a group of registrations is not a
  failing trunk.
- Groups come back largest-first by dialog count.
- `other_count`
  carries everything past `top_n`. So the groups plus it account for
  `total_matched`.
- NER credits a far-end decline (a busy or an explicit reject)
  that ASR does not, per ITU-T E.411.

---

### GET /v1/talkers

The busiest participants, ranked largest first by `ip`, `ua` or `prefix` (the
dialed number's leading digits).

- This is the volume-and-abuse view a dashboard polls.
- No other route exposes it.
- It is the same ranking the MCP `top_talkers` tool
  answers.

**Query parameters:**

- `by` (required) — `ip`, `ua`, or `prefix`. A key outside that set is a `400`.
- `filter` (optional) — a DSL expression or named alias narrowing which
  dialogs count, what `/v1/dialogs?filter=` accepts. A value that is neither is
  a `400`.
- `limit` (optional) — the most rows to return, clamped to the server's row cap.
- `prefix_digits` (optional) — leading digits that make one `prefix` bucket
  (default 4). Zero is a `400`. Ignored for every other `by`.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/talkers?by=ip&limit=10" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "by": "ip",
  "talkers": [
    { "key": "203.0.113.9", "dialogs": 812, "messages": 4123, "invites": 812, "answered": 640, "failed": 121, "share_pct": 67.66 }
  ],
  "truncated": true,
  "distinct_talkers": 47,
  "total_matched": 1200,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**A dialog counts for every participant that took part in it.**

- So `ip` and `ua`
  shares sum above 100%.
- `/v1/aggregate` answers the one-bucket-per-dialog
  question instead.
- Rows rank by dialogs, then messages, then the key. So one
  store always answers in the same order.
- `distinct_talkers` counts every talker.
  So a `limit`-bounded page never reads as the whole ranking.

The `ip` key is the
message SENDER. So a proxy does not top the ranking for calls it only forwarded.

A `ua` key is a banner a stranger typed. It comes back verbatim. So a program
that renders it treats it as untrusted text.

---

### GET /v1/endpoints

Everything one endpoint did, selected by `ip` **or** `user` (exactly one).
This is the
single-participant profile you reach for when a complaint names one phone or one
extension. It reports:

- dialog counts by method and state,
- INVITE outcomes with a failure
  rate,
- REGISTER state,
- the `User-Agent` and `Server` banners it sent,
- the signaling-stack fingerprint read off its request syntax,
- a private-`Contact` rewrite check,
- its RTP streams,
- a bounded page of its most recent dialogs.

These are the same facets the MCP `describe_endpoint` tool reports.

**Query parameters:**

- `ip` (one of `ip`/`user`) — the endpoint's IP address. An address that does
  not parse is a `400`.
- `user` (one of `ip`/`user`) — a SIP URI user part, e.g. `alice`. Matched
  case-sensitively, per [RFC 3261 section 19.1.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3261.html#section-19.1.4).
- `limit` (optional) — the most recent-dialog summaries to return, clamped to the
  server's row cap. The counts always describe every match, not this page.

Neither selector, or both, is a `400`. An endpoint is either an address or a URI
user part. One never implies the other.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/endpoints?ip=203.0.113.9&limit=10" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "endpoint_kind": "ip",
  "endpoint": "203.0.113.9",
  "dialogs": 42,
  "by_method": { "INVITE": 40, "REGISTER": 2 },
  "by_state": { "Completed": 38, "Failed": 4 },
  "messages_sent": 210,
  "messages_received": 198,
  "calls": {
    "invites": 40,
    "with_final_status": 38,
    "failed": 4,
    "failure_rate_pct": 10.53,
    "by_final_status": { "200": 34, "486": 3, "603": 1 }
  },
  "registration": {
    "applicable": true,
    "dialogs": 2,
    "succeeded": 2,
    "failed": 0,
    "auth_loops": 0,
    "problem_call_ids": []
  },
  "user_agents": [
    { "header": "User-Agent", "value": "Grandstream GXP2140 1.0.11.3", "count": 208 }
  ],
  "stack": { "vendor": "grandstream", "confidence": "high" },
  "contact_rewrite": null,
  "streams": {
    "count": 38,
    "orphaned": 0,
    "packets": 152000,
    "lost_packets": 12,
    "max_jitter_ms": 4.7,
    "codecs": ["PCMU", "telephone-event"]
  },
  "recent_dialogs": [
    { "call_id": "a1b2@203.0.113.9", "method": "INVITE", "state": "Completed" }
  ],
  "truncated": true,
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**The counts cover every match. Only `recent_dialogs` is a page.**

- `truncated` is
  true when the endpoint's dialog total exceeds what that page carries.
- An `ip`
  selector reads a socket. So `messages_sent`/`messages_received` count what the
  address sent and received.
- A `user` selector names a party with no socket of its
  own.
  - So both are `0`.
  - Its streams are the ones linked to its dialogs.

Banner
values and codec tokens come back **raw**. These are the values a program keys on.
The MCP surface fences them. `contact_rewrite` is `null` unless the
endpoint sent a REGISTER.

**Security findings are not here.**

- The alert engine
  files them against a source address in a ring this route does not hold.
- So they are the separate `security_findings` capability.

---

### GET /v1/security/findings

What sipnab's own armed detectors recorded, newest first. The detectors are
`scanner`, `fraud`, `digest` and `reg_flood`.

- This is the poll a SOC dashboard makes.
- It is the same ring the MCP `security_findings` tool reads.

**Query parameters:**

- `kinds` (optional) — a comma-separated subset of `scanner`, `fraud`, `digest`,
  `reg_flood`.
  - Omitted returns every kind.
  - Any other name is a `400` naming the
    four.
  - A URL query cannot repeat a key into a list. So the kinds ride in one
    comma-separated value (`kinds=scanner,fraud`).
- `since` (optional) — an RFC 3339 timestamp. The route returns only findings
  recorded strictly after it. A malformed value is a `400`.
- `limit` (optional) — the most findings to return, clamped to the server's row
  cap. `total_matched` still counts every match.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/security/findings?kinds=scanner,fraud&limit=100" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "findings": [
    { "rule_name": "scanner", "src_ip": "203.0.113.9", "detail": "method=OPTIONS ua=sipvicious detection=scanner", "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:00:00+00:00" }
  ],
  "returned": 1,
  "total_matched": 1,
  "truncated": false,
  "armed_kinds": ["scanner"],
  "detection_armed": true,
  "observation_gaps": [],
  "capture_identity": {
    "node": "capture-01",
    "instance": "117b0818df1033d4fd2a28-2",
    "dialog_generation": 13,
    "stream_generation": 2
  }
}
```

**An empty `findings` list is two different states, and `detection_armed` tells
them apart.**

- When it is `false`, this run armed no detector. So nothing could
  have fired.
  - The response then carries a `note` saying exactly that.
  - A reader must NOT take an empty list for a clean bill of health.
- When it is
  `true`, an empty list means the armed detectors saw nothing to report.

Arm a
detector with `--kill-scanner`, `--fraud-detect`, `--digest-leak` or
`--reg-flood`.

**An armed detector can also say it could not see.** `observation_gaps` lists
what it cannot establish from this capture. It is per detector and narrowed by `kinds`.
Each entry is `{ rule_name, reason, seen, unestablished, detail }`.

- `reg_flood`
  files `reason: "no_answers"` when the capture holds REGISTERs and no final
  response to any of them.
- It files `reason: "unanswered"` when some credentialed
  REGISTERs drew no final response inside `--reg-flood-transaction-timeout`.
- An
  empty `findings` beside an entry here means "could not tell", not "clean".
- The entry names no source and never becomes a finding.
- The array is always present.
  It is empty when there is nothing to say.

`total_matched` counts every finding the filter admits across the
whole retained ring (bounded by `--findings-history`). So a `limit`-bounded page
is never mistaken for the whole history.

The `detail` line is a string the
detector built from observed traffic. Its `ua=` half is a banner a stranger
typed.

- It comes back **raw**, the value a program keys on.
- The MCP tool fences it.

---

### GET /v1/captures/compare

Diff two capture files by aggregate. Per dimension, it shows:

- how many dialogs fell in
  each bucket in each capture,
- how far that moved.

The route ranks the rows so "today is worse
than yesterday, and here is where" is the first row.

- This is the query a monitoring
  system polls.
- It is the same diff the MCP `compare_captures` tool answers.

**Query parameters:**

- `a` (required) — the baseline capture, a bare filename inside `--api-file-root`.
- `b` (required) — the capture held against it, a bare filename in the same
  root. A name that resolves to the same file as `a` is a `400`.
- `dimensions` (optional) — a comma-separated subset of the aggregate vocabulary
  (`state`, `response_code`, `method`, `from.user`, `to.user`, `ua`, `src.ip`,
  `dst.ip`, `rtp.codec`). Omitted takes `state` and `response_code`.
- `top_n` (optional) — rows per dimension, clamped to the server's row cap.
  Everything past it sums into an `(other)` bucket.

**Password-protected archives.** `a` or `b` may name a ZIP, encrypted or not.

- sipnab tries the passwords the operator configured at start-up first (see
  [Archives](@/docs/cli.md#archives)).
- A client may add one in the
  `Sipnab-Archive-Password` request header.
- sipnab uses it for that request
  only and never remembers it.

The rules for the header:

- **Only from this host, unless the operator allows more.**
  - sipnab accepts the header from a loopback client: a local tool or a TLS
    proxy on the same host.
  - A remote client gets `403`. That holds when sipnab serves HTTPS itself
    with `--api-tls-cert` too.
  - `--api-accept-archive-passwords` lets remote clients send it. Pass it only
    when TLS encrypts the connection, through `--api-tls-cert` or a TLS proxy
    in front, so the password does not cross the network in the clear.
- **Never in the URL.** A query parameter named like a password gets `400`,
  on every route.
  - The answer advises you to treat that password as exposed.
  - URLs land in proxy and access logs.
- **sipnab limits wrong passwords.**
  - After 5 wrong passwords for one archive
    within 15 minutes, that client gets `429` with `Retry-After` for that
    archive.
  - sipnab counts a client by a fingerprint of its bearer token. It uses
    its address when the client sends none.
  - sipnab logs each wrong password at `warn` with
    that fingerprint, the archive's name and the count.
  - The log never holds the password.
- **No surrounding spaces.** HTTP trims leading and trailing whitespace from
  a header value ([RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html)).
  - So a password that starts or ends with a space
    cannot travel in this header.
  - Configure it on the server instead.
- **No cache keeps a copy.** Some responses carry `Cache-Control:
  no-store`. These are every response to a request carrying the header, and every one that read a password-protected archive.
- **A locked archive answers `422`**, naming `encrypted_no_password` or
  `encrypted_wrong_password` per member. No response repeats the password or
  its length.

`printf` is a shell builtin, so the password never appears in a process list.
`curl -H @-` reads the header from stdin.

```bash
printf 'Sipnab-Archive-Password: %s\n' "$(pass show pcaps/lab)" | curl -s -H @- -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/captures/compare?a=evidence.zip&b=today.pcap" | jq .
```

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/captures/compare?a=yesterday.pcap&b=today.pcap&dimensions=response_code" | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "a": { "filename": "yesterday.pcap", "packets": 41003, "dialogs": 812, "streams": 640, "dialogs_dropped": 0 },
  "b": { "filename": "today.pcap", "packets": 52110, "dialogs": 941, "streams": 733, "dialogs_dropped": 0 },
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "dimension": "response_code",
      "buckets": [
        { "value": "503", "a": 1, "b": 60, "delta": 59 },
        { "value": "200", "a": 700, "b": 690, "delta": -10 }
      ],
      "other": { "value": "(other)", "a": 111, "b": 191, "delta": 80 },
      "distinct_values": 7
    }
  ],
  "summary": "'yesterday.pcap' (812 dialogs) is the baseline; 'today.pcap' (941 dialogs) is held against it, so delta is b minus a. Neither is the capture this server holds."
}
```

**Buckets rank by how far they MOVED, not by how big they are.**

- The largest
  bucket is usually the one that changed least.
- So ranking by movement puts the
  answer first.
- A value present in one capture only reads as zero on the other
  side. "This appeared today" is the finding.
- `dialogs_dropped` above zero
  means that side hit the dialog ceiling. Its counts are a floor.

Bucket values
come back **raw**.

- A `ua` or `from.user` bucket is a banner a stranger typed.
- This route hands a program the value it keys on.
- The MCP tool fences
  those dimensions.

**This route reads files off disk, so it is opt-in.**

- Each name is a bare
  FILENAME, never a path.
- The route refuses a separator, a `..`, or a symlink
  that resolves out of the root.
- A dialog-free file that reported why it read
  nothing is a `422`. It is not a diff whose every bucket collapsed to zero.
- The route answers `503`
  until an operator starts the server with `--api-file-root <DIR>`.

---

### POST /v1/vcon/validate

Check a vCon container against sipnab's vendored schema.

- This is the producer-and-
  conserver boundary.
- There, a store that would refuse a container can warn whoever
  built it first, before it reaches the store.
- It is the one route that validates input
  a caller holds rather than reading the capture.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @container.json http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/vcon/validate | jq .
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 2,
  "verdict": "invalid",
  "schema_id": "https://ietf.org/vcon/schemas/unsigned-vcon.json",
  "schema_path": "tests/schemas/vcon.schema.json",
  "errors": [
    { "instance_path": "", "keyword": "required", "detail": "missing required properties: uuid, created_at" }
  ]
}
```

**`verdict` is `valid` or `invalid`.**

- `valid` is a clean pass.
- `invalid` carries every finding in `errors`.

The schema is the working group's
[draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04 schema](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#appendix-B), vendored unchanged.

The response is `schema_version` 2. A version 1 response also carried
`deviations`, `explanations` and a `valid-except-documented-deviation`
verdict. Version 2 has none of them.

The body must be the JSON object itself, not a string holding it. A non-object
is a `400`.

For a signed, encrypted or gzip format container, sipnab validates the unsigned
vCon inside.

- The body's `Content-Type` is `application/json`, `application/vcon`,
  `application/vcon+json` or, for the gzip format, `application/vcon+gzip`.
  Another is a `400`.
- sipnab opens it with the server's `--vcon-key`, `--vcon-signer-ca` and
  `--vcon-signer-sha256`: see
  [A signed, encrypted or compressed container](@/docs/vcon.md#a-signed-encrypted-or-compressed-container).
- A container that does not open is a `422` with the reason: an encrypted one
  with no `--vcon-key`, a signature that does not verify, a signer the checks
  refuse.

A container whose `critical` lists an extension sipnab does not support is a `422` naming each one.

- sipnab supports `sip-signaling` and `CC`.
- [Section 4.1.4 of draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-04#section-4.1.4) forbids operating on such a container.

The MCP tool `validate_vcon` runs the same validation.

---

### POST /v1/vcon/analyze

Rebuild the SIP messages a stored vCon container holds and analyze them, apart
from the capture this server holds. The answer carries:

- per dialog:
  - the `--json-dialogs` object,
  - the signaling diagnosis,
  - the message ladder,
- the capture analysis.

It reads no store and writes none. The body is the container, in any form
`POST /v1/vcon/validate` takes: sipnab opens a signed, encrypted or gzip
format container first, and one that does not open answers
`verdict: unreadable` with the reason. A gzip format container:

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/vcon+gzip" \
  --data-binary @call.vcon.json.gz 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/vcon/analyze' | jq -c '{verdict, call_id: .dialogs[0].call_id}'
```

```json
{"verdict":"analyzed","call_id":"1-1966@10.0.2.20"}
```

- `limit` (default 50, ceiling
  `--api-max-rows`) bounds the dialogs returned.
- `total_dialogs` counts them all.

**curl**: the container is the one `--export-vcon 1-1966@10.0.2.20 --node-name tap-a` writes from
[`tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/raw/main/tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap). The filter keeps the summary
fields:

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @call.vcon.json "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/vcon/analyze?limit=10" \
  | jq '{verdict, uuid, messages_rebuilt, total_dialogs, truncated, schema_findings, not_recomputed, first_finding: .analysis.findings[0].kind, ladder: [.dialogs[0].ladder[].label]}'
```

**Response:**

```json
{
  "verdict": "analyzed",
  "uuid": "0158a120-0392-857f-8193-d90b5d03d6c4",
  "messages_rebuilt": 6,
  "total_dialogs": 1,
  "truncated": false,
  "schema_findings": [],
  "not_recomputed": [
    "media: a vCon carries no RTP, so no stream, MOS, jitter or loss was computed from it",
    "the producer's analysis holds 1 media_quality row(s), its own numbers, not recomputed",
    "request-URI: not stored for 3 request(s), which carry sip:request-uri-not-stored.invalid",
    "header order: the trace keys headers by name, so their order across names is the container's, not the wire's, and headers the producer did not store (credential headers, when sipnab produced it) are absent"
  ],
  "first_finding": "rebuilt_from_vcon",
  "ladder": [
    "INVITE",
    "100 Trying",
    "200 OK",
    "ACK",
    "BYE",
    "200 OK"
  ]
}
```

**`verdict` is `analyzed` or `unreadable`.**

- `unreadable` means the container
  stores no SIP message sipnab can rebuild, or is not a vCon at all. `reason`
  says which.
- `schema_findings` lists every place the container disagrees with
  the schema, in the shape `POST /v1/vcon/validate` uses.
  - It appears beside either verdict.
  - A finding never stops the analysis.

A container that went through vcon.store,
with `extensions` as an object, still gets an analysis. The section
[A container the schema refuses is still read](@/docs/vcon.md#a-container-the-schema-refuses-is-still-read)
writes `store-shape.vcon.json`:

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @store-shape.vcon.json "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/vcon/analyze" \
  | jq '{verdict, total_dialogs, schema_findings}'
```

```json
{
  "verdict": "analyzed",
  "total_dialogs": 1,
  "schema_findings": [
    {
      "instance_path": "/extensions",
      "keyword": "type",
      "detail": "expected type \"array\", found object"
    }
  ]
}
```

`not_recomputed` lists what a container cannot reproduce.

- A vCon stores no RTP. So sipnab computes no media statistic.
- `stored_media_quality` carries the producer's own numbers verbatim.
- The analysis opens with a
  `rebuilt_from_vcon` finding.

The body must be the JSON object itself, not a string holding it. A non-object
is a `400`. A container whose `critical` lists an extension sipnab does not
support answers `verdict: unreadable`, with a reason naming each one.

The MCP tool [`analyze_vcon`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md#analyze-vcon) runs the
same analysis and answers with the same body. Its section describes every
field.

---

### GET /v1/vcon/spool

The state of the vCon export spool this run writes into. It shows:

- containers pending, delivered and failed,
- for each failed container, the `<name>.error.json`
  record the forwarder wrote beside it. That record holds the store's status and the start of
  its answer.

It reads the directory `--export-vcon-dir` names. It also reads the
forwarder's default `delivered/` and `failed/` directories beside it. A run
started without `--export-vcon-dir` answers `503` naming the flag.

The answer is a snapshot of files on disk, taken when `as_of` says.

- The forwarder (`sipnab --vcon-forward`) is a separate process. It may move a file a
  moment later.
- This route sends, fetches, moves and deletes nothing.
- The MCP
  tool `vcon_spool_status` and `sipnab --vcon-spool-status` give the same
  answer.
- The MCP tool also fences the store's answer as
  untrusted text and cuts it to `--mcp-max-body-bytes`.
- This route returns it as
  the forwarder kept it.

Paging:

- `?limit=` bounds the list of failed records (default 50, ceiling
  `--api-max-rows`).
- `?cursor=` takes the previous answer's `next_cursor`.
- The three counts always describe the whole spool.

A run with several [export rules](@/docs/vcon.md#write-calls-by-rule) writes one
spool per rule.

- `?rule=` names the rule whose spool to read. The flags' rule is
  `--export-vcon-when`.
- With a single spool, a request can leave it out.
- These answer `400` listing the
  run's rule names:
  - several spools and no `rule`,
  - a `rule` the run does not have.
- The answer's `rule` field says which rule's spool it
  describes.

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/vcon/spool?limit=50" | jq .
```

**Response**, from a run started with `--export-vcon-dir vcons` over a spool
holding one container of each kind:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "as_of": "2026-10-12T06:49:34.783Z",
  "note": "A snapshot of files on disk at as_of. ...",
  "spool": { "path": "vcons", "exists": true },
  "delivered_dir": { "path": "vcons/delivered", "exists": true },
  "failed_dir": { "path": "vcons/failed", "exists": true },
  "pending": 1,
  "delivered": 1,
  "failed": 1,
  "failures": [
    {
      "file": "refused.vcon.json",
      "record": {
        "at": "2026-10-11T11:58:02Z",
        "body": "{\"error\":\"vCon already exists\"}",
        "body_truncated": false,
        "file": "refused.vcon.json",
        "method": "POST",
        "reason": null,
        "status": 409,
        "url": "https://vcon.example.com/v1/vcons"
      }
    }
  ],
  "returned": 1,
  "truncated": false,
  "next_cursor": null
}
```

A spool directory that does not exist yet counts as empty, with `exists:
false`: the capture creates it when it writes its first container. `record` is
null when a failed container has no readable record beside it.
`record_problem` then says why.

Only a build with the `vcon`
feature registers this route.

---

### GET /v1/vcon/fetch/:uuid

One vCon container from the operator's vCon store, by uuid, returned in the
answer. sipnab writes no file.

- It connects to the store the `[vcon_fetch]` section of the config file
  configures, so it is off unless the run has `--api-allow-vcon-fetch`.
- The store, its kind, the credential and the decryption key come from
  `[vcon_fetch]` only. The client gives the uuid and nothing else, and the
  answer never holds a key or the credential.
- The request, the credential, the CA, the size limit, the decryption and
  the signer checks are the same as `sipnab --vcon-fetch`
  ([Fetch a stored vCon](@/docs/vcon.md#fetch-a-stored-vcon)).
- The MCP tool [`fetch_vcon`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md#fetch-vcon) gives the same
  answer. Its section describes every field.

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| `200` | The container, with `stored_form`, `decrypted`, `signature_verified`, `signer_sha256` and `schema_findings` |
| `400` | The uuid is not 1 to 64 characters, each a letter, a digit or `-`. sipnab sends nothing |
| `404` | The store answered `404` |
| `502` | Anything else the fetcher refuses: another status, a timeout, an answer over `[vcon_fetch] max_size`, another uuid inside, a key that does not decrypt, a signer that fails a check. `detail` says which, with the credential removed |
| `503` | No `--api-allow-vcon-fetch`, or no `[vcon_fetch] url`; `detail` names the flag or the keys. Also the rate limit |

**curl:**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18080/v1/vcon/fetch/0158a120-0392-8751-9a04-9decf1485b22 \
  | jq -c 'del(.container)'
```

**Response**, from a run started with `--api-allow-vcon-fetch` and a
`[vcon_fetch]` conserver store holding that container, `container` left out:

```json
{"decrypted":false,"schema_findings":[],"schema_version":1,"signature_verified":false,"signer_sha256":null,"stored_form":"unsigned","uuid":"0158a120-0392-8751-9a04-9decf1485b22"}
```

Without the flag:

```json
{"detail":"fetching a vCon from the store is off on this server: start sipnab with --api-allow-vcon-fetch, and configure the store in [vcon_fetch]","status":503,"title":"Service Unavailable","type":"https://sipnab.com/problems/unavailable"}
```

Only a build with the `vcon` feature registers this route.

---

### GET /v1/relay/stats

The relay's own global counters, tiered `relay_reported`.

- It transmits once to the
  address `--rtpengine-control` names.
- It sits behind `--api-allow-relay-query` on a live
  run.

Every response is HTTP 200 with a top-level `outcome`:

- `ok` with the counters,
- or one of the five classifications (`not_configured`,
  `not_permitted`, `unreachable`, `refused`, `suspect`) when no clean answer came
  back.

A refusal is 200, not a 4xx. The route exists. The relay is what did not
answer.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/stats | jq .
```

### GET /v1/relay/stats/names

Which statistics the relay knows.

- sipnab obtains them by asking the relay, not from a table
  built into sipnab.
- So a caller learns what to ask for before a request fails on
  a name this build lacks.
- Names only, no values.
- Same `outcome` envelope and
  same live-source gate as `/v1/relay/stats`.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/stats/names | jq .
```

### GET /v1/relay/stats/call/:call_id

The relay's own counters for one call, by Call-ID, tiered `relay_reported`.

- A relay that does not hold the call answers in its own words.
- sipnab reports that as
  `outcome: refused` with the relay's reason. It does not render it as counters.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/stats/call/1-7@203.0.113.9" | jq .
```

### GET /v1/relay/compare/:call_id

The relay's `totals.RTP.packets` for one call beside sipnab's own measured
count.

- It names both tiers.
- It carries a word verdict and a note.
- The two are never summed.
- A call
  this capture measured no RTP for reads `outcome: not_configured` naming the
  capture.
- A relay that does not hold the call reads `refused`.

Polling on an
interval is not offered over REST at all.

- It is a standing instruction to
  transmit.
- That belongs to the operator who owns the host, i.e. the CLI.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/compare/1-7@203.0.113.9" | jq .
```

---

### GET /v1/relay/holdings

Every Call-ID the live relay is holding right now.

- This TRANSMITS one control
  request.
- So it sits behind `--api-allow-relay-query` on a live source.
- Otherwise it reads
  `not_permitted`/`not_configured`, exactly as the stats routes do.

It closes the gap a passive decoder cannot.

- A call already in progress when sipnab
  started left no control exchange to read.
- That is the case during incident
  response.

These are the same holdings the MCP `query_relay` tool lists. `?max_calls=<N>`
caps the list, and the relay marks the rest `truncated`.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/holdings?max_calls=500" | jq .
```

The body carries `outcome: ok` with `call_ids` and `truncated`, or one of the
five classifications. `outcome` is the field a client branches on first.

---

### GET /v1/relay/holdings/:call_id

What the relay holds for one call:

- each tag it bridges,
- that tag's negotiated
  ports and SSRCs,
- the codec.

It uses the same gate and 200-classification rule as the
list route. It TRANSMITS one control request. It is the same per-call view the
MCP `query_relay` tool returns.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SIPNAB_API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/relay/holdings/1-7@203.0.113.9" | jq .
```

The `call_ids`, tags and ports are the relay's own words. They come back raw, the
values a program keys on.

---

## Add operator notes to a capture

The REST API has no route that reads or writes operator notes. Add notes in
the TUI, or write a pcapng copy of the capture that carries them with
`--notes <FILE> --write-annotated <OUTPUT>`. sipnab does not read packet
comments back from a capture, so no route shows them.

## Status codes

| Code | When |
|------|------|
| `200` | Success |
| `400` | Malformed request (e.g. invalid SSRC on `/v1/streams/{id}`) |
| `401` | Missing/invalid/expired/revoked bearer token |
| `403` | A refused request. The causes: a `Host` header the server does not accept (see [Which `Host` names the API answers](#which-host-names-the-api-answers)); `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` for a dialog that carries the run's `--content-deny-header`; a [`/v1/tfps/` action](#post-v1-tfps-ban) or [`/v1/actions/revert`](#post-v1-actions-revert) when the operator has not enabled actions for REST; an archive password sent from another host to [`/v1/captures/compare`](#get-v1-captures-compare) |
| `404` | Unknown `call_id` or stream id — and every `call_id` on `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}/vcon` in a build without the `vcon` feature, which registers no route at that path |
| `408` | The handler ran past the 30-second per-request cap. Every route sits behind it, so no slow client holds a connection slot open |
| `409` | [`POST /v1/tfps/unban`](#post-v1-tfps-unban) or [`/v1/actions/revert`](#post-v1-actions-revert) for a ban sipnab did not place |
| `413` | A request body larger than 1 MiB (see [Bind address & connection limits](#bind-address-connection-limits)) |
| `422` | The request is well formed but sipnab does not act on it. The causes: a ban address or lifetime the rules do not allow; a vCon container that does not open, or whose `critical` list names an extension sipnab does not support ([`POST /v1/vcon/validate`](#post-v1-vcon-validate)); an audio route for a call with nothing sipnab can decode; a locked or unreadable archive on [`/v1/captures/compare`](#get-v1-captures-compare). `detail` names the reason |
| `429` | An action rate limit, or too many wrong archive passwords from one client on [`/v1/captures/compare`](#get-v1-captures-compare). The answer carries `Retry-After` |
| `500` | The answer would not serialize. Documented on `/v1/dialogs/{call_id}`, its `/report` and `/vcon` variants, `/v1/streams/{id}` and `/v1/report` |
| `502` | The toll-fraud prevention peer a `/v1/tfps/` route asked exited non-zero, hung, or answered off the contract; `detail` carries its standard error |
| `503` | Rejected by the rate limiter or the connection cap (these never answer `429`), or a route this server was not started to serve: [`/v1/captures/compare`](#get-v1-captures-compare) without `--api-file-root`, [`/v1/vcon/fetch/:uuid`](#get-v1-vcon-fetch-uuid) without `--api-allow-vcon-fetch` and `[vcon_fetch]`, an action while sipnab cannot use the actions journal. `detail` names the flag to add |

## Recipes (curl + jq)

Every recipe reads the server address from `$API` and the key from `$KEY`.
Set both in the shell you run the recipes in. Without `$KEY`, every recipe
except the health check returns `401`.

- Set the API address:

   ```bash
   API="http://127.0.0.1:8080"
   ```

- Set your key:

   ```bash
   KEY="my-secret-token"
   ```

Each recipe below is a complete command. Run the one that answers your
question.

Check that the server is up. `/health` is the one endpoint that takes no
credential:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/health"
```

List the failed dialogs:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/dialogs?state=Failed&limit=20" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

List the dialogs from one user (`from=` is a regular expression):

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/dialogs?from=alice&limit=20" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

Get one dialog by Call-ID:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/dialogs/abc123@host" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

Get the same dialog as a JSON call report:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/dialogs/abc123@host/report" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

List only the streams already linked to a dialog:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/streams?orphaned=false" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

List only the streams below a MOS threshold:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/streams?mos_below=3.5" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

Read the aggregate counters and post-dial delay percentiles:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/stats" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq
```

Export every dialog to CSV, for a spreadsheet or a comparison with the
switch's own call records:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/dialogs?limit=1000" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  | jq -r '.dialogs[] | [.call_id, .method, .state, .from_user, .to_user, .duration_sec] | @csv'
```

Against [`tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/raw/main/tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap) it prints:

```text
"completed-9f8e7d@192.0.2.10","INVITE","Completed","alice","bob",20.01
"busy-3a2b1c@192.0.2.30","INVITE","Failed","carol","dave",1.81
"decline-7c6d5e@198.51.100.30","INVITE","Failed","erin","frank",1.81
"notfound-1b2c3d@203.0.113.30","INVITE","Failed","grace","heidi",1.81
"unavail-4e5f60@192.0.2.50","INVITE","Failed","ivan","judy",1.81
```

Print one line per stream with a poor MOS, for an alerting hook. It prints
nothing while every stream is healthy:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/streams?mos_below=3.0" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  | jq -r '.streams[] | "LOW MOS: SSRC=\(.ssrc) MOS=\(.mos) call=\(.associated_dialog)"'
```

Count the dialogs by final response code, one count per call:

```bash
curl -fsS "$API/v1/aggregate?by=response_code" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  | jq -r '.buckets[] | "\(.count)  \(.value)"'
```

```text
1  200
1  404
1  486
1  503
1  603
```

The REST API does not return individual SIP messages. For per-message data,
use the CLI NDJSON mode: `sipnab -N --json` emits one record per message. See
[Output Formats](@/docs/output-formats.md).

## Client examples

The website's API Client Examples page has full end-to-end clients: <https://sipnab.com/docs/api-clients/>.

- They cover bearer auth, pagination, `/metrics` scraping and error handling.
- They are in curl, Python (sync + async), Node/TypeScript, Rust, and Go.

## Security model

- Every network listener binds to loopback by default.
- When you configure a key or a signing key, every route except `/health`
  requires a bearer credential.
  - `/metrics` on the `--api` server takes the same credential.
  - The standalone `--metrics` server uses HTTP Basic instead.
  - Action routes need an `actions` token, and live-audio routes an `audio`
    token.
- Rate limiting applies to every route except `/health`: 100 requests per
  second per source IP by default. `--api-rate-limit-per-peer 0` removes it.
- `--api-max-conn` caps the requests handled at once.
- Key and token comparison runs in constant time.
- Serve HTTPS with `--api-tls-cert` and `--api-tls-key`, or put a reverse
  proxy in front (see [API TLS](#api-tls)).

> **Note:** The API runs as a thread in the sipnab process, not as a separate
> OS process. It does not expose TLS key material. It does expose call
> content: SIP messages inside vCon exports, and decoded audio when the run
> retains it (`--retain-audio`). Two routes change state:
> `POST /v1/persistence`, and the TFPS action routes when `--allow-action`
> enables them.
>
> Choose the API bind address and protect the key accordingly.

### GET /metrics

Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint, documented on its own page:
[Prometheus Metrics](@/docs/metrics.md).

- The endpoints above return what sipnab saw: dialogs, streams, messages.
- `/metrics` returns counters about sipnab itself, in the Prometheus text
  format, for a scraper to poll.
- On the `--api` server it takes the same bearer credential as every other
  route. A `metrics`-scoped token reaches it and nothing else.
